claim: When a Drosophila melanogaster larva encounters a noxious stimulus, such as the focal pressure a parasitic wasp applies to the larval cuticle via its ovipositor, it initiates a characteristic escape response.
source: When a Drosophila melanogaster larva encounters a noxious stimulus, such as the focal pressure a parasitic wasp applies to the larval cuticle via its ovipositor, it initiates a characteristic escape response.
evidence: This is a statement about known behavior of Drosophila larvae in response to noxious stimuli, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The escape sequence consists of an initial abrupt bending, lateral rolling, and finally rapid crawling.
source: The escape sequence consists of an initial abrupt bending, lateral rolling, and finally rapid crawling.
evidence: This describes the sequence of behaviors observed in the escape response, which is established knowledge and also depicted in Figure 1A.

claim: The detection of noxious stimuli primarily relies on class IV multi-dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) located beneath the body wall.
source: Previous work has shown that the detection of noxious stimuli primarily relies on class IV multi-dendritic arborization neurons (Class IV neurons) located beneath the body wall
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Tracey et al., 2003).

claim: The neural mechanisms that underlie the rolling-escape sequence remain unclear.
source: However, the neural mechanisms that underlie the rolling-escape sequence remain unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, indicating a gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Bilateral descending neurons within the subesophageal zone of D. melanogaster larva play a crucial role in regulating the termination of rolling and subsequent transition to escape crawling.
source: Here, we present both functional and anatomical evidence suggesting that bilateral descending neurons within the subesophageal zone of D. melanogaster larva play a crucial role in regulating the termination of rolling and subsequent transition to escape crawling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by functional and anatomical data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The descending neurons designated SeIN128 are inhibitory.
source: We demonstrate that these descending neurons (designated SeIN128) are inhibitory
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing colocalization with GAD (Figure 5A) and functional experiments with VGAT RNAi (Figure 5B-D).

claim: SeIN128 neurons receive inputs from a second-order interneuron upstream (Basin-2) and an ascending neuron downstream of Basin-2 (A00c).
source: and receive inputs from a second-order interneuron upstream (Basin-2) and an ascending neuron downstream of Basin-2 (A00c).
evidence: This claim is supported by connectome data (Figure 4A) and functional calcium imaging experiments (Figure 4B, C).

claim: The ensemble of SeIN128, Basin-2, and A00c neurons forms a GABAergic feedback loop onto Basin-2, which inhibits rolling and thereby facilitates the shift to escape crawling.
source: our findings collectively suggest that the ensemble of SeIN128, Basin-2, and A00c neurons forms a GABAergic feedback loop onto Basin-2, which inhibits rolling and thereby facilitates the shift to escape crawling.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including optogenetic experiments, connectome analysis, and GABA receptor knockdown experiments.

claim: Activation of all Basin neurons (Basin-1, -2, -3, and -4) induced rolling followed by fast crawling.
source: In a previous study, we showed that activation of all Basin neurons (Basin-1, -2, -3, and -4) induced rolling followed by fast crawling (Figure 1A–D; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Upon activation of all Basins, rolling was observed mostly within the first 5 s, followed by crawling.
source: Upon activation of all Basins, we observed rolling mostly within the first 5 s, followed by crawling (Figure 1B (top panel), Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B, C, D.

claim: The crawling speed during activation of all Basins following rolling was ~1.5 times that of the crawling speed at baseline.
source: The crawling speed during activation of all Basins following rolling was ~1.5 times that of the crawling speed at baseline (Figure 1D; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citation to a previous study.

claim: Activation of the split-Gal4 line, SS04185, significantly reduced the probability of rolling when compared to activating only the Basins.
source: we found that activation of the split-Gal4 line, SS04185 (i.e., w1118; R54B01-Gal4AD; R46E07-Gal4DBD), significantly reduced the probability of rolling when compared to activating only the Basins (Figure 1B, C, E, Videos 1 and 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B, C, E and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Activation of SS04185 did not affect the crawling speed during stimulation.
source: without affecting the crawling speed during stimulation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activation of only SS04185 did not induce any extra actions such as crawling, turning, hunching, or stopping.
source: To investigate this possibility, we examined the effect of activating only SS04185 and found that this did not induce any extra actions such as crawling, turning, hunching, or stopping (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: The average time spent rolling was 23.9% (7.2 s out of 30 s) following activation of Basins alone.
source: The average time spent rolling (percentage of the 30 s stimulation period) was 23.9% (7.2 s out of 30 s) following activation of Basins alone
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: The average time spent rolling was only 5.9% following co-activation of Basins and SS04185 (1.8 s out of 30 s).
source: whereas it was only 5.9% following co-activation of Basins and SS04185 (1.8 s out of 30 s) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The duration of each rolling bout was significantly shorter when SS04185 neurons were co-activated with Basins.
source: Additionally, the duration of each rolling bout was significantly shorter when SS04185 neurons were co-activated with Basins (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.001; Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Co-activating the Basins and SS04185-expressing neurons only marginally increased latency to onset of the first rolling bout.
source: Compared to activating Basins alone, co-activating the Basins and SS04185-expressing neurons only marginally increased latency to onset of the first rolling bout (Figure 1G)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Co-activating the Basins and SS04185-expressing neurons markedly reduced the latency for the termination of rolling.
source: whereas it markedly reduced the latency for the termination of rolling (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.001; Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SS04185-expressing neurons are involved in terminating rolling.
source: These data strongly suggest that SS04185-expressing neurons are involved in terminating rolling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing reduced latency to termination of rolling.

claim: Co-activation of SS04185 and Basins resulted in the initiation of the first crawling bout occurring earlier than when only Basins were activated.
source: Co-activation of SS04185 and Basins resulted in the initiation of the first crawling bout occurring earlier than when only Basins were activated (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.001; Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The time from the end of rolling to the start of crawling remained similar between the groups in which the Basins were activated alone and in which the Basins and SS04185 were co-activated.
source: The time from the end of rolling to the start of crawling remained similar between the groups in which the Basins were activated alone and in which the Basins and SS04185 were co-activated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Activation of SS04185 neurons in conjunction with Basins did not change the crawling speed compared to activation of Basins alone.
source: Lastly, activation of SS04185 neurons in conjunction with Basins did not change the crawling speed compared to activation of Basins alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: SS04185 activation terminates rolling and facilitates the shift to fast crawling.
source: These results collectively indicate that SS04185 activation terminates rolling and facilitates the shift to fast crawling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of behavioral data.

claim: SS04185 split-Gal4 strongly labeled a pair of descending neurons located within the SEZ and mushroom body (MB) neurons within the brain.
source: We found that SS04185 split-Gal4 strongly labeled a pair of descending neurons located within the SEZ and mushroom body (MB) neurons within the brain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Activation of SS04185 neurons with reduced SS04185-MB expression still reduced rolling probability to a level no different from that of KZip− controls expressing SS04185 fully in both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons.
source: When compared to KZip+ controls, which do not express SS04185 (Figure 2C, black bars), however, activation of SS04185 neurons with reduced SS04185-MB expression (Figure 2C, red bars on the right; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) still reduced rolling probability (as well as the total duration of rolling [Figure 2—figure supplement 1C]) to a level no different from that of KZip− controls expressing SS04185 fully in both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons (Figure 2C, dark red bars in the middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Co-activation of MB Gal4 lines (MB247-Gal4) with Basins (without activation of SS04185-DN neurons) did not reduce the probability of rolling.
source: Additionally, co-activation of MB Gal4 lines (MB247-Gal4) with Basins (without activation of SS04185-DN neurons) did not reduce the probability of rolling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: SS04185-DN neurons inhibit rolling.
source: These data indicate that SS04185-DN neurons inhibit rolling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing that reducing MB expression does not affect the inhibition of rolling.

claim: Knockdown of SS04185-MB neurons did not increase the duration of rolling bouts.
source: As a result, knockdown of SS04185-MB neurons did not increase the duration of rolling bouts (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The earlier onset of crawling triggered by the activation of SS04185 neurons remained the same with knockdown of SS04185-MB neurons.
source: Furthermore, the earlier onset of crawling triggered by the activation of SS04185 neurons remained the same with knockdown of SS04185-MB neurons (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The behavioral effects on both rolling and crawling are primarily mediated by SS04185-DN neurons.
source: Collectively, these results strongly suggest that the behavioral effects on both rolling and crawling, as illustrated in Figure 1, are primarily mediated by SS04185-DN neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence showing that MB neurons are not responsible for the observed effects.

claim: Activation of both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons resulted in a reduction in both the probability and duration of rolling when compared to activation of SS04185-MB neurons alone.
source: Remarkably, activation of both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons resulted in a reduction in both the probability and duration of rolling when compared to activation of SS04185-MB neurons alone (Figure 2F, G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from FlpOut experiments shown in Figure 2F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: Activation of both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons reduced the latency to the end of the first rolling bout and the initiation of the first crawling bout.
source: Furthermore, activation of both SS04185-MB and SS04185-DN neurons reduced the latency to the end of the first rolling bout and the initiation of the first crawling bout (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1J.

claim: A single pair of descending neurons in SS04185 is important for termination of rolling during the activation of Basins.
source: Collectively, the results suggest that a single pair of descending neurons in SS04185 is important for termination of rolling during the activation of Basins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FlpOut experiments and other data.

claim: SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons are one and the same.
source: Our immunostaining data also showed that the cell bodies of SS04185-DN neurons are located in the SEZ, with axons bilaterally innervating the medial regions of the ventral nerve cord (VNC) from the thoracic to abdominal segments A8/9 (Figure 2A), suggesting that SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons are one and the same.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of immunostaining data with EM reconstruction data, showing similar anatomical features.

claim: The projections of SeIN128 neurons are distributed within the ventromedial neural tract in Drosophila larvae.
source: We confirmed that the projections of SeIN128 neurons are distributed within the ventromedial neural tract (one of the six major neural tracts) in Drosophila larvae (Figure 3A–C) in EM reconstruction data.
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: The cell bodies of SS04185-DN neurons were located in the SEZ region, where the most anterior of the three neuropils in the thoracic region was marked by N-cadherin.
source: We also confirmed that the cell bodies of SS04185-DN neurons were again located in the SEZ region, where the most anterior of the three neuropils in the thoracic region was marked by N-cadherin (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Immunostaining with Fasciclin2 (Fas2) showed colocalization of the axonal projections of SS04185-DN neurons and the Fas2-labeled ventromedial tract.
source: Immunostaining with Fasciclin2 (Fas2), which labels various neural tracts in the VNC (Grenningloh et al., 1991; Santos et al., 2007), showed colocalization of the axonal projections of SS04185-DN neurons and the Fas2-labeled ventromedial tract (Figure 3C, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C, E and citations to previous work.

claim: The similarity of the locations of their cell bodies and the distributions of their axonal processes suggests the identity of the SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons.
source: The similarity of the locations of their cell bodies and the distributions of their axonal processes suggests the identity of the SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on anatomical comparisons.

claim: SeIN128 neurons were located downstream of Basin neurons.
source: A previous EM study showed that SeIN128 neurons were located downstream of Basin neurons (Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous EM study.

claim: Basin projections colocalize with those of SS04185-DN neurons in both the horizontal and transverse planes.
source: Immunostaining revealed that Basin projections colocalize with those of SS04185-DN neurons in both the horizontal and transverse planes (Figure 3F, top and lower panels, respectively)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SS04185-DN projections are distributed slightly medial to those of Basins within the ventromedial tract.
source: with the horizontal view showing that SS04185-DN projections are distributed slightly medial to those of Basins within the ventromedial tract (Figure 3F, top panels), which resembles their colocalization pattern reported in EM (Figure 3B, C, G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F and comparison with EM data in Figure 3B, C, G.

claim: The projections of A00c colocalize with those of SS04185-DN in a similar fashion along the rostrocaudal axis within the ventromedial tract.
source: Similarly, we compared the distributions of SS04185-DN projections with those of A00c or mdIV projections. We found that the projections of A00c colocalize with those of SS04185-DN in a similar fashion along the rostrocaudal axis within the ventromedial tract (Figure 3H,I)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: A00c projections are distributed more medially than SS04185-DN projections.
source: with A00c projections distributed more medially than SS04185-DN projections, consistent with the distribution patterns of SeIN128 projections and A00c projections in the EM reconstruction dataset (Figure 3B, H, I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and comparison with EM data shown in Figure 3B, H, I.

claim: The distributions of mdIV projections did not colocalize with those of SS04185-DN projections.
source: In contrast, the distributions of mdIV projections did not colocalize with those of SS04185-DN projections, as the mdIV projections were displaced more laterally relative to the SS04185-DN projections in the horizontal and transverse planes (Figure 3J, top and lower panels, respectively)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The projections of SS04185-DN neurons were distributed dorsomedial to those of mdIV in the transverse plane.
source: In the transverse plane, the projections of SS04185-DN neurons were also distributed dorsomedial to those of mdIV (Figure 3J, lower panel), consistent with the corresponding distribution patterns in the EM reconstruction dataset (Figure 3B, C, K).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data and comparison with EM data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3B, C, K.

claim: The morphological findings for SS04185-DN neurons, together with data on the distribution of their axonal projections in relation to that of Basin, A00c, and mdIV neurons, strongly suggest the identity of SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons.
source: We conclude that the morphological findings for SS04185-DN neurons, together with data on the distribution of their axonal projections in relation to that of Basin, A00c, and mdIV neurons, strongly suggest the identity of SS04185-DN and SeIN128 neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of anatomical evidence.

claim: Basin-2 and A00c neurons make excitatory synaptic contacts onto SeIN128 neurons.
source: A previous study that reconstructed larval neurons involved in the rolling circuit showed that Basin-2 and A00c neurons (in the VNC) make excitatory synaptic contacts onto SeIN128 neurons (in the CNS)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Ohyama et al., 2015) and connectome data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SeIN128 neurons make reciprocal inhibitory synaptic contacts onto Basin-2 and A00c neurons.
source: which in turn make reciprocal inhibitory synaptic contacts onto Basin-2 and A00c neurons (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and connectome data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SeIN128 neurons are directly activated by Basin-2 and A00c.
source: These data suggest that SeIN128 neurons are directly activated by Basin-2 and A00c (which also receives inputs from Basin-1, Basin-2, and Basin-4).
evidence: This is an inference based on the connectome data showing synaptic connections.

claim: GCaMP signals in SeIN128 neurons increased in an intensity-dependent manner when either Basins and A00c were activated.
source: GCaMP signals in SeIN128 neurons increased in an intensity-dependent manner when either Basins and A00c were activated (Figure 4B, C)
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Peak activity in SeIN128 neurons occurred at around 3 s after the onset of LED stimulation when Basins or A00c neurons were stimulated.
source: Peak activity occurred at around 3 s after the onset of LED stimulation, which was similar to the results when Basins or A00c neurons were stimulated (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B, C.

claim: Both Basin and A00c stimulation resulted in linear dose-dependent increases in SeIN128 firing.
source: Finally, both Basin and A00c stimulation resulted in linear dose-dependent increases in SeIN128 firing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SeIN128 neurons are downstream of Basins and A00c neurons.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that SeIN128 neurons are downstream of Basins and A00c neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the calcium imaging data showing that SeIN128 responds to activation of Basins and A00c.

claim: A00c neurons displayed a similar dose-dependent increase in peak axonal firing as the intensity of optogenetic stimulation of Basin neurons increased.
source: Although A00c neurons displayed a similar dose-dependent increase in peak axonal firing as the intensity of optogenetic stimulation of Basin neurons increased
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Unlike SeIN128 neurons, A00c neurons showed no delay in peak firing activity.
source: unlike SeIN128 neurons they showed no delay in peak firing activity (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A00c and SeIN128 neurons function differently in the rolling circuit.
source: suggesting that A00c and SeIN128 neurons function differently in the rolling circuit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different temporal dynamics of their responses.

claim: The outgoing projections of SeIN128 neurons primarily make synaptic contacts along the anterior–posterior nerve axis.
source: We then investigated the anatomical locations of the synaptic outputs and inputs of SeIN128 neurons, and found that, whereas their outgoing projections primarily make synaptic contacts along the anterior–posterior nerve axis
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The inputs coming from other neurons to SeIN128 are mainly located in the SEZ.
source: the inputs coming from other neurons are mainly located in the SEZ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SeIN128 neurons make axo-axonal contacts onto Basin-2 neurons.
source: On the other hand, SeIN128 neurons make axo-axonal contacts onto Basin-2 neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–G) as well as A00c neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–G.

claim: SeIN128 axons make synaptic contacts with the dorsal and medial processes of Basin-2, which correspond to their axonal compartments.
source: that is, their axons make synaptic contacts with the dorsal and medial processes of Basin-2, which correspond to their axonal compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E–G.

claim: The delay of SeIN128 activity may be caused by multi-synaptic connections involving the SEZ or a feedback loop involving axo-axonal connections between SeIN128 and Basin-2 or A00c.
source: These data suggest that the delay of SeIN128 activity may be caused by multi-synaptic connections involving the SEZ or a feedback loop involving axo-axonal connections between SeIN128 and Basin-2 or A00c.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed delay in SeIN128 activity.

claim: SeIN128 neurons colocalized with glutamic acid decarboxylase (Gad)-positive neurons.
source: To test this possibility, we performed immunostaining experiments and found that SeIN128 neurons colocalized with glutamic acid decarboxylase (Gad)-positive neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SeIN128 neurons did not colocalize with acetylcholine- or glutamate-positive neurons.
source: but not with acetylcholine- or glutamate-positive neurons, suggesting that SeIN128 neurons are GABAergic inhibitory neurons (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: SeIN128 neurons are GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
source: suggesting that SeIN128 neurons are GABAergic inhibitory neurons (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on immunostaining data showing colocalization with GAD and lack of colocalization with markers for other neurotransmitters.

claim: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via HMS02355 increased the population-level rolling probability from 23.6% to 45.2%.
source: When we expressed RNA interference (RNAi) HMS02355 in SeIN128 neurons to knock down vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) expression and suppress the release of GABA, the population-level rolling probability increased from 23.6% to 45.2% (Figure 5B, C; Kallman et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B, C and citations to previous work.

claim: Pan-neural HMS02355 expression decreased GABA and VGAT expression in the neuropil.
source: We confirmed the effect of HMS02355 by immunostaining: pan-neural HMS02355 expression decreased GABA and VGAT expression in the neuropil (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: The duration of each bout of rolling increased from 0.8 to 1.4 s when VGAT was knocked down in SeIN128 neurons.
source: Furthermore, the duration of each bout of rolling increased from 0.8 to 1.4 s (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SeIN128 neurons inhibit rolling via GABAergic transmission.
source: These data support the idea that SeIN128 neurons inhibit rolling via GABAergic transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the VGAT knockdown experiments.

claim: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via TNT while triggering rolling by optogenetically activating Basin neurons significantly increased the probability of rolling compared to controls.
source: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via TNT while triggering rolling by optogenetically activating Basin neurons via R72F11-LexA>LexAop-CsChrimson significantly increased the probability of rolling compared to controls (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via TNT extended the duration of each rolling bout, as well as the total rolling duration, in each larva.
source: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via TNT extended the duration of each rolling bout, as well as the total rolling duration, in each larva (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: The time to offset of rolling and the time onset of crawling were both delayed relative to controls upon silencing SeIN128 neurons.
source: We also examined the rolling-escape crawling sequence upon silencing SeIN128 neurons, and found that the time to offset of rolling and the time onset of crawling were both delayed relative to controls (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E, F.

claim: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via shibirets1 increased the probability of rolling from 60.4% to 79.7%.
source: Silencing SeIN128 neurons via shibirets1 increased the probability of rolling from 60.4% to 79.7% (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The total duration of rolling per animal during stimulation increased from 10 to 12 s when SeIN128 neurons were silenced via shibirets1.
source: The total duration of rolling per animal during stimulation increased from 10 to 12 s (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The time to offset of the first rolling bout was delayed relative to controls when SeIN128 neurons were silenced via shibirets1.
source: the time to offset of the first rolling bout was delayed relative to controls (p = 0.013 for Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The activity of SeIN128 neurons is important in controlling the duration of rolling and the shift to crawling.
source: Together with the results showing that activation of SeIN128 neurons inhibits rolling, these findings suggest that the activity of SeIN128 neurons is important in controlling the duration of rolling and the shift to crawling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from activation and silencing experiments.

claim: Knockdown of ionotropic GABA-A receptors (GABA-A-R) and G-protein-coupled GABA-B receptors (GABA-B-R1 and GABA-B-R2) in Basin neurons increased the rolling probability at the population level from 80% to 90% or even higher.
source: For all RNAi lines, the rolling probability at the population level increased from 80% to 90% or even higher (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: All GABA receptor knockdown groups showed significant increases in rolling duration across multiple bouts.
source: while the total rolling duration at the individual level increased for each larva throughout the stimulation window (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A). All GABA receptor knockdown groups showed significant increases in rolling duration across multiple bouts (Figure 7B)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All groups except for GABA-B-R11 showed a reduced time to onset of the first rolling bout.
source: all groups except for GABA-B-R11 showed a reduced time to onset of the first rolling bout (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only the GABA-B-R2 and GABA-A-R groups showed a delayed offset of the first rolling bout.
source: and only the GABA-B-R2 and GABA-A-R groups showed a delayed offset of the first rolling bout (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: None of the GABA receptor knockdown groups differed from controls in the time to onset of the first crawling bout.
source: None of the groups differed from controls in the time to onset of the first crawling bout (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The greatest increase in the probability and duration of rolling was seen during knockdown of ionotropic GABA-A-R (Rdl).
source: The greatest increase in the probability and duration of rolling was seen during knockdown of ionotropic GABA-A-R (Rdl), suggesting that Rdl contributes most to the inhibition of Basin neurons (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Rdl contributes most to the inhibition of Basin neurons.
source: suggesting that Rdl contributes most to the inhibition of Basin neurons (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that GABA-A-R knockdown had the greatest effect.

claim: Basins in the experimental group showed reductions in GCaMP signaling by 11–36% compared to those in the control group.
source: We found that Basins in the experimental group showed reductions in GCaMP signaling by 11–36% compared to those in the control group (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The reductions in Basin GCaMP signaling were observed at all stimulation intensities when contrasting peak GCaMP responses, and statistically significant at intensities of 0.3 and 0.5 µW/mm2.
source: The reductions were observed at all stimulation intensities when contrasting peak GCaMP responses, and statistically significant at intensities of 0.3 and 0.5 µW/mm2 (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: SeIN128 neurons directly inhibit the activity of Basins via GABA.
source: Collectively, these data support the idea that SeIN128 neurons directly inhibit the activity of Basins via GABA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including GABA receptor knockdown and calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Of the four types of Basins, only Basin-2 and Basin-4 receive nociceptive input from mdIV and trigger rolling.

claim: Feedback inhibition occurs when an excitatory neuron sends projections to an inhibitory neuron, which in turn sends projections back onto the same excitatory neuron, often at its presynaptic terminals.
source: Feedback inhibition occurs when an excitatory neuron sends projections to an inhibitory neuron, which in turn sends projections back onto the same excitatory neuron, often at its presynaptic terminals (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Kapfer et al., 2007; Ray et al., 2020; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005).
evidence: This is a definition of feedback inhibition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The hallmark of feedback inhibition lies in its ability to modulate the duration and magnitude of incoming excitatory signals, thereby fine-tuning neural responses and maintaining homeostasis.
source: The hallmark of feedback inhibition lies in its ability to modulate the duration and magnitude of incoming excitatory signals, thereby fine-tuning neural responses and maintaining homeostasis (Kapfer et al., 2007; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the function of feedback inhibition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The temporal dynamics of feedback inhibition are slower than feedforward inhibition, primarily due to the added synaptic delays (two or more) following activation of an excitatory neuron.
source: Compared to the fast temporal dynamics of feedforward inhibition, in which an inhibitory neuron directly inhibits an excitatory neuron downstream of it, the temporal dynamics of feedback inhibition are slower, primarily due to the added synaptic delays (two or more) following activation of an excitatory neuron (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Ray et al., 2020; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the temporal properties of feedback inhibition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The slow temporal dynamics of feedback inhibition serve to inhibit the sustained neural activity and magnitude of incoming excitatory signals.
source: The slow temporal dynamics serve to inhibit the sustained neural activity and magnitude of incoming excitatory signals (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Ray et al., 2020; Stokes and Isaacson, 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the function of the slow temporal dynamics of feedback inhibition supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SeIN128 neurons are descending neurons whose main inputs arrive in the brain and SEZ regions, and whose outputs target the VNC.
source: In this study, we showed that SeIN128 neurons are descending neurons whose main inputs arrive in the brain and SEZ regions, and whose outputs target the VNC.
evidence: This is a summary of anatomical findings from the study.

claim: SeIN128 neurons receive excitatory inputs from Basin-2 as well as its downstream neuron A00c, and in turn send inhibitory projections back to these neurons in the VNC, potentially establishing a feedback inhibition motif that modulates the nociceptive rolling circuit.
source: We also found that SeIN128 neurons receive excitatory inputs from Basin-2 as well as its downstream neuron A00c, and in turn send inhibitory projections back to these neurons in the VNC, potentially establishing a feedback inhibition motif that modulates the nociceptive rolling circuit.
evidence: This is a summary of connectome and functional findings from the study.

claim: The interplay observed among SeIN128 neurons, Basin-2, and A00c is consistent with the view that feedback inhibition is critical in regulating the temporal aspects of nociceptive responses.
source: The interplay we observed among SeIN128 neurons, Basin-2, and A00c is consistent with this view. Our findings revealed that activation of SeIN128 neurons has a suppressive effect on Basin-2 activity and, notably, on the duration of rolling. These observations support the idea that feedback inhibition is critical in regulating the temporal aspects of nociceptive responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Axo-axonal synapses have a subtle effect on neurotransmission at the network level because the activity in presynaptic neurons does not alter the membrane potential.
source: Axo-axonal synapses have a subtle effect on neurotransmission at the network level because the activity in presynaptic neurons does not alter the membrane potential (Cattaert and El Manira, 1999; Guo and Hu, 2014; McGann, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of axo-axonal synapses supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Axo-axonal synapses mainly affect the release probability of neurotransmitter vesicles in response to an action potential triggered in the postsynaptic neuron.
source: Axo-axonal synapses mainly affect the release probability of neurotransmitter vesicles in response to an action potential triggered in the postsynaptic neuron (McGann, 2013; Oleson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of action of axo-axonal synapses supported by citations to previous work.
